entries.clue: Office of the President, where a load of balls may be witnessed (4)

annotation.definition2: where a load of balls may be witnessed
annotation.definitionNote: Neither half is a plain synonym of the answer: the President's room is known by the shape of it and the cricket ground by the shape of the field, so the word stands in each case as a name rather than a description.

blocks.note: the room in the West Wing where an American president works, known by its shape

blocks.clueFragment: where a load of balls may be witnessed
blocks.note: a Test cricket ground by Vauxhall in south London, where deliveries are bowled all summer

annotation.surface: The White House office as a place where an enormous amount of nonsense gets talked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A load of balls' is the dismissive phrase the surface wants and the literal count the second definition needs. The comma after 'President' looks like a pause in one sentence and is actually the seam between two whole clues.
annotation.definitionFit: The President's room and the south London cricket ground are both named for their shape, so one word names each.

entries.clue: One very contorted bra's pressure line (6)

indicatorNotes.contorted: Something contorted has been twisted out of its proper shape, so the three letters beside it are not standing in the order printed.

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
so hot and very hot say the same thing, so the two words trade freely
the three letters of the garment, twisted into another order

annotation.surface: A badly twisted bra and the line of pressure it leaves behind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very' looks like an intensifier attached to 'contorted' and is a separate two-letter piece of its own. Weather charts draw these lines through every place whose barometer agrees.
annotation.definitionFit: An isobar is the line a weather map runs through all the points recording the same atmospheric pressure.

entries.clue: Cry: "Women are sick!" (4)

blocks.note: w is the letter on the door of the ladies'
to ail is to be unwell

annotation.surface: An outcry at the news that the women have all gone down with something.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon and the exclamation mark dress the second half up as reported speech, which is exactly what a cry would be. Nothing in the clue admits that the first word is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To wail is to cry aloud in grief, and the noun and the verb both answer to it.

entries.clue: Indian cookery clubs of Estonia? (6)

blocks.note: a balti is a curry cooked and brought to the table in its own steel bowl, a Birmingham invention
c is the card player's short form for clubs

annotation.surface: Curry houses and nightclubs somewhere in an Estonian city.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is apologising for naming a whole region by one of the three countries in it. 'Clubs' sits beside a restaurant and belongs to a pack of cards.
annotation.definitionFit: Estonia is one of the three Baltic states, so the adjective for the whole region is defined by a single instance of it.

entries.clue: Wealthy American goes after Will's character (10)

indicatorNotes.goes after: What goes after a thing follows it, so the short piece named first in the clue is written last, behind the long one.

blocks.note: the exiled duke who works the magic in Shakespeare's The Tempest
US is the everyday short form for American

annotation.surface: A rich American trailing round after one of Shakespeare's creations.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Will' is Shakespeare on first-name terms, a habit worth learning because setters use it constantly. The clue reads left to right while the answer assembles the other way, which is what 'goes after' is there to warn you about.
annotation.definitionFit: Prosperous means thriving and comfortably off, which is what calling somebody wealthy says.

entries.clue: Marks and Spencer's chief at AGM  it's chaotic (8)

indicatorNotes.chief: The chief of a word is the letter at its head, so only the first letter of the name before it is taken.
indicatorNotes.chaotic: Chaos is the absence of any arrangement at all, so the letters gathered up in front of it hold no order of their own.

blocks.note: the letter standing at the head of the name
the little word taken exactly as printed
the three letters of the annual general meeting, taken as printed
the pronoun taken exactly as printed

annotation.surface: A high-street retailer's boss making a shambles of the annual general meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Marks and Spencer's chief' reads as one man running one shop and splits straight down the middle, the definition on one side and a single letter on the other. Stigmata are the wounds of the Crucifixion, reappearing on the hands and feet of saints.
annotation.definitionFit: Stigmata are marks on the body, so the plural noun answers the plural noun.

entries.clue: Balls after tense jog (4)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the word opening the clue takes second place.

blocks.note: t is the grammarian's short form for tense
rot is talk not worth listening to

annotation.surface: Nonsense talked after somebody's nervous little run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' and 'rot' are both words for nonsense, which is the sense the wordplay wants and not the one the capital letter at the front of the clue invites. Tense is a property of verbs before it is a mood.
annotation.definitionFit: A trot is a gentle run, which is what a jog is; both work as noun and as verb.

entries.clue: Eye-related American reversal in medication aid? (6)

indicatorNotes.reversal: A reversal turns a thing end for end, so the two letters just named are written the other way about.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the pair goes into the middle of the word named after them.

blocks.note: a vial is the small glass bottle a dose of medicine arrives in
US is the short form for American, arriving here back to front

annotation.surface: An American policy U-turn over a piece of medical kit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eye-related' is the magazine printing the puzzle winking at itself, and it is the definition rather than any part of the picture. The question mark admits that a vial is a container rather than an aid.
annotation.definitionFit: Visual means belonging to sight, which is the eye's business.

entries.clue: Teller's list Republican managed to overturn (8)

indicatorNotes.to overturn: To overturn a thing is to tip it upside down, and in an across entry that means the whole assembly is read back from its right-hand end.

blocks.note: a rota is the list saying whose turn it is
r is the standard short form for Republican, as on an American ballot
to run a department is to manage it

annotation.surface: A bank cashier's duty roster that a Republican contrived to get thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Teller' is the bank counter on the surface and the storyteller in the definition. All three pieces go in facing forwards and the finished run is turned round once at the end, rather than each piece separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrator is the one who tells the story, so teller names the job exactly.

entries.clue: Our ex-PM "right off the French"  scrap (6)

indicatorNotes.off: Taking something off is taking it away, so the letter just named comes out of the word in front of it.

blocks.note: Liz Truss, Britain's Prime Minister for seven weeks in the autumn of 2022
r is the standard short form for right, as in a stage direction
le is one of the French words for the

annotation.surface: A former Prime Minister dropping her rightwing politics along with the French.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'right off the French' look like one soundbite and hide the join: the first word is a letter to lose, the last two a word to gain. French articles are standard crossword currency — LE, LA, UN, UNE.
annotation.definitionFit: A tussle is a rough physical struggle, and a scrap is that same scuffle under a more casual name.

entries.clue: Private Eye would rather not have one be ill dancing at clubs (5,4)

annotation.definition: Private Eye would rather not have one
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a synonym for it: 'one' stands in for the thing itself, and Private Eye is the magazine this puzzle appears in, dragged through the defamation courts for decades.

indicatorNotes.dancing: A dancer never stays put, so letters told to dance will not be standing where they were printed.

blocks.note: the five letters of these two words, shaken into a new order
clubs are one of the four suits in a pack of cards

annotation.surface: Somebody too unwell to be out dancing in nightclubs.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the setter's own shop talking, which is why it runs to six words where most clues manage one. 'Clubs' is a card suit and not a nightclub, and it is the only word here that could have been either.
annotation.definitionFit: A libel suit is the action for defamation that a satirical magazine spends its life trying to avoid.

entries.clue: This is about grabbing money  which makes sense (5)

indicatorNotes.is about: To be about is to be turned round, so the little word in front is read from its last letter back to its first.
indicatorNotes.grabbing: To grab a thing is to close your hand round it, so the letters already settled take in what comes next.

blocks.note: the four letters of the word itself, read from the back
a G is a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

annotation.surface: Getting hold of money is what the whole thing is about, and that is only reasonable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This' is fodder rather than a pointer to anything outside the clue, which is the hard part — four letters to be turned round. The definition is the noun 'sense', one of the five, doing duty inside the verb phrase 'makes sense'.
annotation.definitionFit: Sight is one of the five senses, so 'sense' defines it by the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: (&15/17) Yet forecast starts off with "fire Burnham's close colleague!" (5)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters told they are off have turned too: not one of them stays where it was printed.

blocks.note: seventeen letters from these three words, every one of them used
four more letters thrown onto the same pile

annotation.surface: A weather forecast that opens by demanding the sacking of the mayor's closest ally.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starts off with' reads as one phrase meaning 'begins with', and only the middle word of it is an instruction. Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July 2026, which is what makes his closest colleague a cabinet rank rather than a friend.
annotation.definitionFit: The First Secretary of State outranks the rest of the cabinet as the Prime Minister's de facto deputy, and Andy Burnham is that Prime Minister.

entries.clue: Base weakness of speaker (5)

annotation.surface: A fault in the way somebody speaks.
annotation.walkthrough: The Speaker of the Commons is the decoy, and the floor is where members speak. The two words only sound alike in British English, where that final r is left unsounded.
annotation.definitionFit: The floor is the base of a room, the surface everything else in it stands on.

entries.clue: They could well be toxic, contemptible types and dicks (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a clause about the answer rather than a synonym for it: it states the one thing the name is meant to warn you of, since the word marks no botanical category of its own.

tool is the same playground insult as dick, and both started from the same anatomical joke

annotation.surface: A roll-call of unpleasant people, with a warning that they may be poisonous as well.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are playground insults, which is this setter's register throughout the puzzle. 'Types' looks like a category word and is doing nothing of the kind — it is only what makes the toads plural.

entries.clue: see 13ac. (9)

the four letters of the untruth, resettled

entries.clue: Material of robe forced round arse (7)

entries.clue: Charitable African country protecting government leader (6)

the letter standing at the head of that word

entries.clue: Quiet, extreme leftwinger's piece (5)

entries.clue: Old president Trump needs to change party (6)

entries.clue: Old Hollywood star's flipping tabloid stink (5)

indicatorNotes.flipping: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the word after it is read from its last letter back to its first.

entries.clue: MAGA means suppressing contest (4)

entries.clue: A living ruined by the heartless anti-migrant activist? (9)

the definite article with its central letter taken out

entries.clue: US enforcers going after "Liberal lousy things" (4)

entries.clue: All but advanced peer (4)

entries.clue: Butcher's dog cut one on behind (8)

indicatorNotes.cut: A cut takes the end off, so the dog's name is written with its last letter gone.

blocks.note: a mutt is a mongrel, here docked of its final letter
the Roman numeral for one
a train running behind is running late

entries.clue: Eye's description of comical leader given the boot (6)
